title: The Family as a System: Roles, Stocks and Feedback Loops
topic: tư duy: tư duy hệ thống qua gia đình
unit: Chặng 1/12 · Ngôi nhà & gia đình Việt · Tuần 1/4: Gia đình, họ hàng & xưng hô
summary: Systems thinking looks at elements, interconnections and purpose, at stocks that fill and drain, and at balancing and reinforcing feedback loops. Applied to a Vietnamese family, it shows why behavior often belongs to the role rather than the person, and where small leverage points can shift a stuck pattern.
body:
Picture a family lunch on the anniversary of a grandfather's death (*đám giỗ*). The eldest son's wife is in the kitchen before dawn. The younger brothers arrive late and carry the tables. An aunt notices that the youngest daughter-in-law has not been seated and quietly fixes it. Nobody wrote a rulebook for this, yet everyone seems to know their part, and the day runs. When something goes wrong, say two brothers stop speaking over a plot of ancestral land (*đất hương hỏa*), the whole lunch feels it, even people who have nothing to do with the land.

That is what a system looks like from the inside. This piece introduces one thinking tool, **systems thinking**, and uses a Vietnamese family as the worked example.

## What a system is

The environmental scientist Donella Meadows, in her short book *Thinking in Systems: A Primer* (2008), defined a system as "an interconnected set of elements that is coherently organized in a way that achieves something." Textbooks that follow her break this into three parts:

- **Elements**: the parts. In a family, the people: grandparents, parents, children, in-laws, cousins. Elements can also be intangible, such as the family's reputation in the village or its savings.
- **Interconnections**: what Meadows called "the relationships that hold the elements together." In a family these are obligations, money flows, who-calls-whom, who must be consulted, and the address terms that mark rank (*vai vế*).
- **Purpose or function**: what the whole tends to produce. For a traditional Vietnamese family, part of the purpose has long been raising children, caring for the old, and keeping the ancestral altar going.

A useful test from one conservation textbook: many parts can sit side by side, but "unless they depend on and interact with each other, they are simply a collection." A crowd at a bus stop is a collection. A family is a system.

The key move in systems thinking is to pay at least as much attention to the interconnections and purpose as to the elements. We tend to explain events by pointing at a person: "the problem is that daughter-in-law," "the problem is that uncle." Systems thinking asks instead: what arrangement of roles and pressures makes this behavior likely, whoever is standing in that role?

## Stocks and flows

Two more words make the idea concrete.

A **stock** is something that accumulates and can be measured at a point in time: water in a tank, money in an account. Stocks change only through **flows**: inflows add, outflows drain.

A family has stocks too. Some are tangible: savings, land, the number of working-age adults living nearby. Some are softer but just as real: trust between siblings, a mother's energy, a family's standing in the commune. Each has inflows and outflows. Trust between two brothers grows with every favor returned and every visit home at Tết; it drains with every slight, every unequal division of care for an aging parent.

Thinking in stocks explains why families change slowly and then suddenly. Resentment can build for years without anyone noticing, like water rising behind a dam. Then a small event, a remark at a wedding, a disputed will, releases it all at once. The remark gets the blame, but the stock had been filling for a decade.

## Feedback loops: the engine of behavior

A **feedback loop** is a closed chain of cause and effect that runs from a stock back to itself. There are two kinds.

**Balancing loops** hold a stock near a target. A thermostat is the classic example: the room gets cold, the heater turns on, the room warms, the heater turns off. Families are full of balancing loops. When a grandmother falls ill, children who live far away visit more often; when she recovers, visits drop back. When one sibling carries too much of the caregiving, the others feel the pressure from relatives' gossip and step in. Balancing loops are why families are stable and resistant to change, for better and for worse.

**Reinforcing loops** amplify change. The more there is, the more there will be: a "virtuous" or "vicious" cycle. Consider a common pattern in Vietnamese families today. Grown children move to the city for work. With fewer young people in the village, there are fewer reasons for the next cousins to stay. More leave. Each departure makes leaving easier for the next person. Or the reverse, a virtuous loop: an elder sister who succeeds in her studies becomes a model and a source of help for younger siblings, who then succeed and help the ones after them.

Most real behavior comes from several loops interacting. That is why "just tell people to behave differently" rarely works: you are pushing against loops that keep pulling the system back.

## Roles: why the same person acts differently in different seats

Here is the most useful practical insight for a Vietnamese reader. In a family, people occupy **roles** (*vai*) that come with expectations attached: the eldest son (*con trưởng*), the daughter-in-law (*con dâu*), the youngest child (*con út*), the elder branch versus the younger branch (*con bác, con chú*). Many behaviors belong more to the role than to the person.

The same woman can be a quiet, careful daughter-in-law in her husband's family and a confident, outspoken eldest sister in her own. The same man may be the decision-maker at his office and the one who fetches the tea at his father's house. Nothing about their character changed. The seat changed.

The American psychiatrist Murray Bowen, whose family systems theory was first published in 1966, built a whole framework on this observation. Two of his eight core concepts are especially handy:

- **Triangles.** When tension rises between two people, they tend to pull in a third to relieve it. Think of a mother and daughter-in-law who do not speak directly but send messages through the son. The son ends up in the middle of a triangle, and the original problem never gets addressed.
- **Differentiation of self.** Bowen's term for the ability, as one summary puts it, "to think as an individual while staying meaningfully connected to others." A well-differentiated person can disagree with the family without cutting ties, and stay close without being swept along by every anxiety.

You do not need to accept all of Bowen's theory to find these two ideas useful as lenses.

## Applying it: one problem, two explanations

Take a familiar dispute. An elderly father lives alone in the village after his wife dies. Three adult children live in different cities. Months pass; the father grows frail; the siblings argue about who should do more.

**The person-centered explanation:** the eldest son is irresponsible; the daughter is too far away; the youngest is selfish.

**The systems explanation:** look at the structure.
1. *Roles.* Tradition expects the eldest son (*trưởng nam*) to take responsibility, but he may be the one with the least flexible job. The daughter "belongs to another family" by old custom, so she may hold back even if she lives closest in practice.
2. *Stocks.* The father's health is a stock that has been draining slowly. Sibling trust is another stock, already low from an earlier quarrel over land.
3. *Loops.* A balancing loop exists: when the father is in crisis, everyone rushes home. But it only fires in emergencies, so the slow drain continues between crises. Meanwhile a reinforcing loop of blame runs: each sibling's absence makes the others resentful, which makes them less willing to coordinate, which leads to more gaps.
4. *Triangles.* The siblings talk about each other through their father, who is caught in the middle.

The systems view does not excuse anyone. It changes what you try. Instead of a one-time lecture to the "bad" sibling, you look for a **leverage point**, a place where a small change shifts the pattern. Meadows wrote at length about such points. Here they might be a regular, shared rota agreed in a family video call; one sibling taking the role of coordinator; or paying a neighbor or relative nearby to check in daily, turning an emergency-only loop into a steady one.

## Three cautions

Systems thinking is a lens, not a verdict. Use it with care.

- **It can sound cold.** Calling your mother an "element" will not win you friends at Tết. Keep the vocabulary in your head and speak in ordinary words.
- **Structure is not destiny.** Roles push, but people choose. A differentiated person can step out of a triangle.
- **Every map leaves things out.** A loop diagram is a simplification. As Meadows herself put it, "the universe is messy."

## How to practice

1. **Draw one loop a week.** Pick a pattern you see at home or at work, such as "the more my colleague is late, the more others cover for her, the less she needs to be on time." Draw it as arrows in a circle. Is it balancing or reinforcing?
2. **Find the stock.** For any recurring tension, ask: what is slowly filling or draining here? Trust, energy, money, goodwill?
3. **Swap the person for the role.** When someone annoys you, ask: "Would almost anyone in that seat act this way?" If yes, the problem is in the structure.
4. **Spot a triangle.** Notice the next time someone tells you about a third person instead of talking to that person directly. You may be the third corner.

Families are the first system any of us learns. Learning to see yours as one, with roles, stocks and loops, is a quiet way to become both kinder and more effective inside it.

unsure: Meadows quotes were checked through secondary sources (a university textbook and a conservation journal), not the book itself.
Bowen family systems theory is influential in family therapy but its concepts are not all strongly supported by experimental research; here it is used as a lens, not as settled science.

connect.why: Systems thinking is one more model for the latticework: the family is the first place to hang it.
The shrinking household and the money and care flowing between city and village are stocks and loops in the same family system.
Address terms are the visible interconnections of the family system; choosing them well is adjusting your role inside it.

check.q: What are the three parts of a system in Meadows' framing, and what would each be in a Vietnamese family?
check.a: Elements (the people, plus things like savings or reputation), interconnections (obligations, money flows, rank and address terms) and purpose (raising children, caring for elders, keeping the ancestral altar).

check.q: Explain the difference between a balancing and a reinforcing loop with one family example each.
check.a: A balancing loop pulls a stock back toward a target, e.g. children visit more when a parent is ill and less when she recovers. A reinforcing loop amplifies change, e.g. each young person leaving the village makes leaving easier for the next.

check.q: What does 'swap the person for the role' mean, and how does it change your response to a family conflict?
check.a: Ask whether almost anyone in that seat would act the same way; if so, the cause is structural, so you look for a leverage point (a rota, a coordinator, a triangle to step out of) rather than blaming one person.

try: This week, pick one recurring pattern at home or at work and draw it as a loop of arrows. Label it balancing or reinforcing, and name the stock that is filling or draining.
